Bayesian data augmentation [@tanner_calculation_1987] is a computational strategy that expands the parameter space by introducing latent variables,
so that a likelihood intractable on the observed data alone becomes tractable on the "augmented data", observed and latent variables.

For example, consider a single infected individual $i$.
Imagine that someone reported the date of symptom onset $d^\mathrm{ons}_{i}$.
We can think of the observation process that returned that value as some function of the true onset time, $t^\mathrm{ons}_{i}$.
Then, we introduce a latent infection time $t_{i}$, defined as the difference between the onset time and the latent incubation period $\tau^\mathrm{inc}_{i}$, so that $t^\mathrm{ons}_{i} = t_{i} + \tau^\mathrm{inc}_{i}$, where the incubation period is modelled according to some prior knowledge, or depending on some parameters to be inferred.

Like parameters, latent variables need a model (possibly the transmission model itself) and a proposal for the MCMC sampler.
Latent variable definitions may depend on another definition in the model:
another latent variable, a data column, an observation, a group rate or a parameter.
A model looks the name up among its definitions, so each name must stand for one of them only^[A name nothing declares is an error, reported when the model is run, and so is a name claimed by two definitions.].
Names combine into arithmetic expressions, such as `onset_date - incub_period` or `exposure_max + 0.99`, and can be passed to any of the functions listed by `browse_functions()`, e.g. `sqrt(beta)` or `floor(onset_time)`.

The sections below show how to define such individual latent variables on minimal examples.

# Status-specific definitions

In many applications, the same latent variable has to be augmented according to different rules depending on the individual.
Infection times of symptomatic and asymptomatic members are one example.
Status-specific definitions apply to one status only, while generic definitions hold for every positive status.
Consider a survey that follows a household for 10 days from the first symptom onset, testing every member at the start and at the end of follow-up.
We tag symptomatic members with `status = 1` and asymptomatic ones with `status = 2`.
We augment infection times of symptomatic members as shown in [Get Started](housepi.html), informed by the reported onset date.
For asymptomatic members we sample the infection time within the follow-up period:
```{r}
#| label: status-specific-latent
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)
set.seed(42)

onset_tommy <- 5
hh_model <- data.frame(id = c("tommy", "gina"), hh_id = "house_1",
                       start_date = onset_tommy, end_date = onset_tommy + 10,
                       status = c(1, 2),  onset_date = c(onset_tommy, NA)) |>
  new_housepi_model("case-ascertained") |>
  add_parameter(alpha = 0.001, beta = 0.07, gamma = 0.9, hh_size_ref = 4) |>
  add_infectivity_profile(import = "template") |>
  # associate latent definitions
  add_latent(
    # latent infection time for symptomatic members,
    # using a generic definition
    infec_time = onset_date - incub_period,
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1),
    # latent infection time for asymptomatic members,
    # using a status-specific definition, with priority over generic
    infec_time = list(status = 2, min = start_date, max = end_date)
  )
```
For case-ascertained models, infection times are modelled by transmission, so they take no `model`.

To check how the latent draws evolve, pass the `id` of the individuals to follow to the argument `id_draws` of `run_inference()`.
```{r}
#| label: latent-infection-time-plot
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Density plots of latent infection times for two household members.
# run inference following traces of specific individuals
hh_model |>
  # store latent draws of "tommy" and "gina"
  run_inference(id_draws = c("tommy", "gina")) |>
  get_latent_draws("infec_time") |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_hist(facet_args = list(ncol = 1), alpha = 0.5, binwidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(data = data.frame(xintercept = onset_tommy),
             aes(xintercept = xintercept)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = onset_tommy + c(-10, 10))
```
Gina's infection time cannot precede the start of follow-up (Tommy's onset), and the model makes it more probable close to that bound.

The model keeps the last step of its last running chain, and `inspect_augmented_data()` adds those latent values to the dataset:
```{r}
#| label: inspect-augmented-data
inspect_augmented_data(hh_model)
```
Tommy's infection time is his onset date minus his incubation period, while Gina carries no incubation period, as her definition does not read one.

# Estimate latent model parameters

Consider a synthetic report of the days when each case was exposed to infection and of the day of symptom onset.
We simulate it with the "test" model (see `?template_test`), which carries no transmission dynamics,
by chaining latent variables and observations for each individual:

- the exposure window lasts 1 to 4 days, and its last day `exposure_max` is an observation drawn from a categorical distribution (the draw is 0-based, so `exposure_max` counts the days after the first);
- the infection time `infec_time` is uniform within the exposure window;
- the incubation period `incub_period` is gamma distributed with the `mean` and `sd` we want to recover later;
- the reporting delay `report_offset` is symmetrical of -1, 0 or 1 day.

The observations produce the reported columns:
the last day of exposure, drawn from its model, and the reported onset day `onset_day`, computed from the onset time and the reporting delay.
```{r}
#| label: generate-delays-data
true_params <- c(mean = 2.2, sd = 1.2)
dataset <- data.frame(hh_id = seq_len(223), status = 1) |>
  new_housepi_model("test") |>
  add_parameter(import = true_params) |>
  add_latent(
    # infection time uniform within the reported exposure window
    # min = 0 by default for uniform, max + 1 spans the whole last day
    infec_time = list(model = "uniform", max = exposure_max + 1),
    # incubation period gamma by mean/std. deviation
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", mean = mean, sd = sd),
    # reporting delay in days
    report_offset = list(model = "categorical", 0.2, 0.6, 0.2),
  ) |>
  add_observation(
    exposure_max = list(model = "categorical", 0.28, 0.34, 0.26, 0.12),
    onset_day = floor(infec_time + incub_period) + report_offset - 1
  ) |>
  run_simulation() |>
  # keep the reported columns only
  dplyr::select(id, hh_id, status, exposure_max, onset_day)
head(dataset)
```
The data has no household structure, so every individual lives in a household of their own.

We then imagine we received such a dataset and, assuming a gamma-distributed incubation period,
we want to estimate its `mean` and `sd` by augmenting the infection times and the incubation periods.

For inference we keep the "test" model, which has no transmission term, and build the augmentation definitions for:

- the infection time `infec_time`, drawn uniformly within the reported exposure window;
- the incubation period `incub_period`, gamma distributed with the `mean` and `sd` to be inferred.

Finally, an observation ties the reported `onset_day` to the onset time `infec_time + incub_period`.
`onset_day` counts whole days, so we set `discr = TRUE`, and the probability of day $k$ is the mass the normal law puts on $[k, k + 1)$.
The reporting delay is symmetric around 0, so we centre the normal law on the onset time and let its `sd` absorb the delay.

```{r}
#| label: incubation-example
#| fig-height: 3
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for mean and standard deviation parameters with three parallel chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
# generate an instance of the household model class
hh_fit <- dataset |>
  new_housepi_model("test") |>
  # define the gamma distribution parameters to be inferred
  add_parameter(mean = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 4),
                sd = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 4)) |>
  # latent variable definitions
  add_latent(infec_time = list(model = "uniform", max = exposure_max + 1),
             incub_period = list(model = "gamma", mean = mean, sd = sd)) |>
  # observation model for the reported onset day
  add_observation("onset_day", discr = TRUE, model = "normal",
                  mean = infec_time + incub_period, sd = 0.5) |>
  # store latent draws of "7" and "13"
  run_inference(id_draws = c("7", "13"))

# plot traces of parameter draws
true_table <- data.frame(parameter = names(true_params), true = true_params)
hh_fit |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace() +
  geom_hline(data = true_table, aes(yintercept = true))
```

The draws of the latent variables `infec_time` and `incub_period` are stored for individuals "7" and "13", here the incubation periods:
```{r}
#| label: latent-draws-traces
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for individual latent variables across three MCMC chains.
#|  Incubation period for two subjects (IDs 7 and 13).
# plot the traces of the incubation period alone
hh_fit |>
  get_latent_draws("incub_period") |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```

If a latent variable is not read by any observation or transmission term, housepi does not sample it and it carries no trace.
